quickStart: For an immediate emergency involving police, fire, or ambulance, call 111.
For urgent health advice that is not an emergency, call Healthline on 0800 611 116.
For poison advice, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766.
For brief emotional support, call or text 1737. If someone is in immediate danger, call 111.
Review emergency contacts, health information, legal document locations, insurance, bank accounts, KiwiSaver, pensions, and essential liabilities.
Use official bereavement and provider processes. Do not access accounts or use credentials without authority.
Keep the export encrypted and never store passwords, PINs, myIR/RealMe credentials, authentication codes, or recovery keys in it.

legalNotes: This guide is general information, not legal, tax, insurance, or financial advice.
Publicly funded health and disability services have eligibility rules. ACC is a separate scheme for injuries and acceptance and support depend on its rules.
A New Zealand EPA for property and an EPA for personal care and welfare are distinct. EPA authority ends on death; an executor's authority comes from the will and any required court grant.

Estate administration, probate, tax, relationship property, and trust questions can depend on the facts and may require High Court or professional steps. Confirm with Govt.nz, Inland Revenue, and a qualified New Zealand adviser.
Poison advice: National Poisons Centre: https://poisons.co.nz/

fileStructure: The export ZIP may contain a spreadsheet, PDFs, and this access guide.
Treat every file as sensitive; it may include identity, health, financial, and legal references.
dataAccess: Extract to a private, encrypted location and keep an untouched backup.
Share only with trusted authorised people; a family relationship alone does not grant legal access.
Store credentials in a reputable password manager with an emergency-access feature, not in this export.
securityTips: Never put passwords, PINs, IRD portal credentials, authentication codes, or recovery keys in the export.
Use encrypted storage and secure channels for sensitive documents.
Review after major life events and at least annually; remove outdated copies securely.

recoveryRoadmap.description: A general checklist after a death in New Zealand. Confirm representative authority and current legal, tax, and provider requirements before acting.

meta.title: Family Recovery Roadmap - New Zealand
meta.reviewedBy: Government sources reviewed; individual legal and tax advice may be needed

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This checklist is intended to make the first practical steps clearer.
intro.howToUse: Follow official registration guidance, identify the executor or administrator, notify relevant agencies and providers, and keep a record of each action.

startHere: Follow the official death-registration and certificate process.
Locate the will and identify the executor; check whether a High Court grant or other authority is required.
Notify Inland Revenue, Work and Income, ACC, banks, insurers, employers, and KiwiSaver or pension providers as appropriate.
List assets, debts, regular bills, and claims; confirm responsibility before changing payments or distributing property.
Keep a log of contacts and documents supplied. Never use another person's myIR, RealMe, banking, or device credentials.
legalFramework: Govt.nz death, wills, probate, and estate processes.
Inland Revenue final individual and estate tax responsibilities.
Different enduring powers of attorney for property and personal care and welfare; an EPA does not appoint an executor and ends on death.
KiwiSaver, NZ Super, ACC, insurance, relationship property, and trust rules depend on programme and personal circumstances.

phases.title: Register and establish authority
phases.focus: Follow registration instructions, locate the will, and identify who may act.

keyActions.action: Follow the official registration process and obtain the death certificate or records required by providers.
keyActions.why: The registrar and each institution set the applicable evidence requirements.

keyActions.action: Find the will and confirm the executor; seek advice if there is no will, an overseas asset, or a dispute.
keyActions.why: The executor or court-appointed administrator has duties and may need a grant before dealing with assets.

mustHaveDocuments: Bank, KiwiSaver, insurance, property, and debt references
criticalMistakes: Assuming next of kin automatically has authority
Treating an EPA as continuing after death
Putting passwords or recovery codes in an exported record

phases.title: Notify and identify claims
phases.focus: Notify government agencies and providers and keep an accurate estate inventory.

keyActions.action: Contact Inland Revenue and other relevant government agencies using current bereavement processes.
keyActions.why: Tax, payments, and entitlements may need to be updated; requirements depend on the situation.

keyActions.action: Contact banks, insurers, employers, lenders, KiwiSaver providers, and utilities separately.
keyActions.why: Government notification does not complete private-provider claims or account administration.

mustHaveDocuments: List of recurring bills and liabilities
criticalMistakes: Assuming an asset passes outside the estate

phases.title: Administer and finalise
phases.focus: Complete the court, tax, property, and provider work required for this estate.

keyActions.action: Confirm whether probate or letters of administration are needed and follow the High Court process when required.
keyActions.why: The process depends on the estate and the organisations holding assets.

keyActions.action: Confirm final tax and estate income obligations with Inland Revenue or a qualified tax adviser before distribution.
keyActions.why: The estate can have ongoing income and filing responsibilities.

mustHaveDocuments: Grant or administration papers if required
criticalMistakes: Distributing assets before confirming court and tax obligations
Assuming no estate tax or filing duties apply
Using the deceased person's account credentials

phases.title: Review family arrangements
phases.focus: Review the surviving household's estate, KiwiSaver, insurance, and secure information arrangements.

keyActions.action: Review wills, enduring powers, beneficiaries, insurance, and emergency contacts with appropriate professionals.
keyActions.why: Major life changes can make current appointments or nominations unsuitable.

keyActions.action: Keep an asset and digital-account index; store credentials only in a suitable password manager.
keyActions.why: A secure index helps authorised people locate records without exposing secrets.

criticalMistakes: Leaving old appointments or beneficiaries in place
Storing credentials in a spreadsheet or PDF

estate.note: Check the will, executor, and whether probate or letters of administration are required.

healthEligibility.note: Eligibility for publicly funded health services depends on status and programme rules; ACC is a separate accident injury scheme.

glossary.definition: A person named in a will who is responsible for administering the estate, subject to applicable law and any required grant.
A legal appointment for property or personal care and welfare decisions during a person's lifetime; it is separate from a will and does not continue after death.
A High Court grant confirming an executor's authority to administer an estate when required.
